In SCOPe 2.08 ferritins, ribonucleotide-reductase-like proteins, and manganese catalases are three separate families inside one superfamily, the Ferritin-like superfamily a.25.1 (sunid 47240), within the Ferritin-like fold a.25 (sunid 47239) in class a (all-alpha). Their relationship is therefore a superfamily-level one: divergent evolution from a common ancestor, with the different chemistries explained as functional divergence of homologous proteins rather than as convergence or chance structural similarity.

The specific placements are: Ferritin family a.25.1.1 (sunid 47241; includes apoferritin, bacterioferritin, Dps-type dodecameric ferritin homologs, and the rubrerythrin/nigerythrin N-terminal domains), Ribonucleotide reductase-like family a.25.1.2 (sunid 47253; includes RNR R2, soluble methane monooxygenase alpha and beta subunits, toluene/o-xylene monooxygenase subunits, stearoyl-ACP desaturase, and PaaC), and Manganese catalase (T-catalase) family a.25.1.3 (sunid 100951, cross-referenced to Pfam PF05067). The superfamily also holds YciF-like, half-ferritin, PMT1231-like, MiaE-like, Rv2844-like families, and an automated-matches family a.25.1.0. Pairwise comparison of representative domains confirms the relationship: human H-chain ferritin d1fhaa_ versus E. coli RNR R2 d1riba_, d1riba_ versus Lactobacillus plantarum Mn catalase d1jkua_, and d1fhaa_ versus d1jkua_ all resolve to lowest shared node a.25.1 (same_superfamily, no caveats or heterogeneity flags), not to any family.

What each level means here. (1) Fold a.25 is only a structural statement: core of four helices, closed left-handed-twist bundle with one crossover connection. The fold also contains superfamilies that SCOPe does not consider homologous to ferritins, e.g. Cobalamin adenosyltransferase-like a.25.2, EsxAB dimer-like a.25.3, PE/PPE dimer-like a.25.4, HP0062-like a.25.5, SO2669-like a.25.6; sharing the fold with these does not imply common ancestry. (2) Superfamily a.25.1 is the homology statement. SCOPe's annotation for it, 'contains bimetal-ion centre in the middle of the bundle', names the shared feature that justified grouping the families despite low sequence identity: a conserved di-metal site built from carboxylate (Glu/Asp) and His ligands on the four-helix bundle, at equivalent positions. That is the classic SCOP criterion for remote homology: structural similarity plus a conserved functional site location and ligand chemistry, not sequence alone. (3) Family level separates them because they have diverged far in sequence and in chemistry: ferritins use a diiron 'ferroxidase' centre to oxidize Fe(II) and store iron inside a 24-mer (or 12-mer Dps) shell; RNR R2 and the bacterial multicomponent monooxygenases/desaturases use a diiron (or Mn/Fe) centre to activate O2 for radical generation or hydrocarbon oxidation; manganese catalases use a dimanganese centre to disproportionate H2O2. The ancestral feature retained is the bimetal site and its helical scaffold; the metal identity, redox partner, substrate, and oligomeric assembly have all diverged.

Limits on interpretation. The superfamily assignment supports shared ancestry but does not license transfer of function, substrate, metal identity, or mechanism across families: a new ferritin-like-fold protein that hits an RNR R2 template should not be annotated as a ribonucleotide reductase, a ferritin, or a catalase from the structural match alone. Even within the Ribonucleotide reductase-like family, members are desaturases, monooxygenases, and a radical-generating RNR subunit, so family membership itself does not fix function. Assigning a novel sequence to one of these families requires family-level evidence beyond fold recognition: significant sequence or profile similarity to the family (e.g. Pfam PF05067 for Mn catalase versus the ferritin or RNR R2 families), conservation of the specific metal-ligand residues and metal type, and ideally biochemical data; structure-only or AlphaFold-based hits to a.25 representatives establish at best a candidate superfamily hypothesis. Also note that SCOPe places several multi-subunit diiron oxygenases in a.25.1.2 by domain, and many newer entries are in automated-matches nodes (a.25.1.0 and per-family 'automated matches' protein nodes) whose assignments were made by sequence similarity to curated representatives rather than by manual curation, so representative choice and the release (2.08) matter when citing these groupings. Membership in another a.25 superfamily (e.g. EsxAB or PE/PPE dimers, which form the four-helix bundle only as dimers and lack the bimetal site) must not be read as homology to ferritins.

In SCOPe 2.08 ferritins, ribonucleotide-reductase-like proteins, and manganese catalases are three separate families inside one superfamily, the Ferritin-like superfamily a.25.1 (sunid 47240), within the Ferritin-like fold a.25 (sunid 47239) in class a (all-alpha). Their relationship is therefore a superfamily-level one: divergent evolution from a common ancestor, with the different chemistries explained as functional divergence of homologous proteins rather than as convergence or chance structural similarity.

The specific placements are: Ferritin family a.25.1.1 (sunid 47241; includes apoferritin, bacterioferritin, Dps-type dodecameric ferritin homologs, and the rubrerythrin/nigerythrin N-terminal domains), Ribonucleotide reductase-like family a.25.1.2 (sunid 47253; includes RNR R2, soluble methane monooxygenase alpha and beta subunits, toluene/o-xylene monooxygenase subunits, stearoyl-ACP desaturase, and PaaC), and Manganese catalase (T-catalase) family a.25.1.3 (sunid 100951, cross-referenced to Pfam PF05067). The superfamily also holds YciF-like, half-ferritin, PMT1231-like, MiaE-like, Rv2844-like families, and an automated-matches family a.25.1.0. Pairwise comparison of representative domains confirms the relationship: human H-chain ferritin d1fhaa_ versus E. coli RNR R2 d1riba_, d1riba_ versus Lactobacillus plantarum Mn catalase d1jkua_, and d1fhaa_ versus d1jkua_ all resolve to lowest shared node a.25.1 (same_superfamily, no caveats or heterogeneity flags), not to any family.

What each level means here. (1) Fold a.25 is only a structural statement: core of four helices, closed left-handed-twist bundle with one crossover connection. The fold also contains superfamilies that SCOPe does not consider homologous to ferritins, e.g. Cobalamin adenosyltransferase-like a.25.2, EsxAB dimer-like a.25.3, PE/PPE dimer-like a.25.4, HP0062-like a.25.5, SO2669-like a.25.6; sharing the fold with these does not imply common ancestry. (2) Superfamily a.25.1 is the homology statement. SCOPe's annotation for it, 'contains bimetal-ion centre in the middle of the bundle', names the shared feature that justified grouping the families despite low sequence identity: a conserved di-metal site built from carboxylate (Glu/Asp) and His ligands on the four-helix bundle, at equivalent positions. That is the classic SCOP criterion for remote homology: structural similarity plus a conserved functional site location and ligand chemistry, not sequence alone. (3) Family level separates them because they have diverged far in sequence and in chemistry: ferritins use a diiron 'ferroxidase' centre to oxidize Fe(II) and store iron inside a 24-mer (or 12-mer Dps) shell; RNR R2 and the bacterial multicomponent monooxygenases/desaturases use a diiron (or Mn/Fe) centre to activate O2 for radical generation or hydrocarbon oxidation; manganese catalases use a dimanganese centre to disproportionate H2O2. The ancestral feature retained is the bimetal site and its helical scaffold; the metal identity, redox partner, substrate, and oligomeric assembly have all diverged.

Limits on interpretation. The superfamily assignment supports shared ancestry but does not license transfer of function, substrate, metal identity, or mechanism across families: a new ferritin-like-fold protein that hits an RNR R2 template should not be annotated as a ribonucleotide reductase, a ferritin, or a catalase from the structural match alone. Even within the Ribonucleotide reductase-like family, members are desaturases, monooxygenases, and a radical-generating RNR subunit, so family membership itself does not fix function. Assigning a novel sequence to one of these families requires family-level evidence beyond fold recognition: significant sequence or profile similarity to the family (e.g. Pfam PF05067 for Mn catalase versus the ferritin or RNR R2 families), conservation of the specific metal-ligand residues and metal type, and ideally biochemical data; structure-only or AlphaFold-based hits to a.25 representatives establish at best a candidate superfamily hypothesis. Also note that SCOPe places several multi-subunit diiron oxygenases in a.25.1.2 by domain, and many newer entries are in automated-matches nodes (a.25.1.0 and per-family 'automated matches' protein nodes) whose assignments were made by sequence similarity to curated representatives rather than by manual curation, so representative choice and the release (2.08) matter when citing these groupings. Membership in another a.25 superfamily (e.g. EsxAB or PE/PPE dimers, which form the four-helix bundle only as dimers and lack the bimetal site) must not be read as homology to ferritins.
